input: Liquid-liquid extraction offers an effective route for recovering acetone from an aqueous stream by contacting it with an organic solvent, and the design considered here is based on a countercurrent cascade. The cascade is arranged so that the aqueous stream and the solvent pass one another through the stages, with the freshest solvent meeting the most depleted aqueous stream at the end of the cascade. The distribution coefficient for acetone between the organic and aqueous phases is 1.87 at 25 °C, which indicates a favourable partitioning of the acetone into the solvent phase. The design uses 5 countercurrent stages, and on this basis the predicted recovery is 93% of the acetone in the feed, representing a high level of separation for a relatively modest number of stages. It is important to note, however, that this prediction rests on two assumptions that should be borne in mind when interpreting the figure. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages throughout the cascade, and it also assumes negligible mutual solubility between the two phases. Neither of these assumptions has been checked on the actual solvents involved, so the predicted recovery should be treated as an estimate that remains to be confirmed in practice, rather than as a guaranteed level of performance for the unit as it will actually be built and operated in the plant.
target: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetone from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient, organic over aqueous, is 1.87 at 25 °C. With 5 countercurrent stages, the predicted recovery is 93% of the acetone in the feed. A distribution coefficient above unity puts most of the acetone in the solvent at each contact, and countercurrent flow keeps the leanest solvent against the leanest aqueous stream, so the driving force is held along the cascade; the recovery figure is the result of the coefficient and the stage count together, not of either alone. The stages are counted as equilibrium stages: each stage is credited with the full separation the coefficient allows at the compositions the stage actually sees, and no allowance is made for incomplete contacting within a stage. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages. A real stage falls short of equilibrium by an amount that depends on the contacting device, and the recovery of the built unit would fall short of the prediction by the corresponding amount. The prediction also assumes negligible mutual solubility of the two phases. Solvent lost to the aqueous raffinate, or water carried into the extract, would move both the recovery and the downstream loads. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. The recovery figure is a prediction on stated assumptions, to be replaced by a measured recovery when the actual solvents have been run.
